title: 22. Interview: Consistency Models
summary: Interview Q&A for Consistency Models — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Consistency Models interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Define linearizability in one sentence and explain why it implies consensus.
**Answer:** Linearizability is the guarantee that every operation appears to take effect atomically at a single point in real time between the operation's invocation and its response, so concurrent operations form a total order that respects real-time precedence. The reason it implies consensus is that agreeing on this single point in time across replicas requires the replicas to agree on a value — and the FLP impossibility result shows that asynchronous consensus cannot be both safe and always live under crash failures. The practical implication is that any linearizable store must run a consensus protocol (Raft, Paxos, Zab, Viewstamped Replication) on every write that affects the linearization point, and quorum-based linearizable reads must touch enough replicas to guarantee they overlap the latest write. This is why linearizability is expensive — every operation pays the cost of consensus — and why engineers reach for weaker models whenever the application tolerates staleness.
**Visual:**
```
real time  ----w1(x=1)----r1--------r2---->
                  |        |         |
single point:     @t1    @t2(=1)  @t3(=1)
requires consensus on every linearization point
```

### Q2. What is the difference between sequential consistency and linearizability? Give a concrete example where they diverge.
**Answer:** Sequential consistency requires that there exists a single total order of all operations such that each client's program order is preserved and each read returns the value written by the most recent write in that total order; it does *not* require that this total order respect real-time ordering between clients. Linearizability adds the real-time constraint: if operation A completes before operation B starts in wall-clock time, then A must precede B in the total order. Concretely: client 1 writes X=1 and finishes at t=100ms; client 2 starts a read of X at t=200ms. Under linearizability, client 2 *must* see X=1. Under sequential consistency, client 2 may see X=0 as long as *every* client agrees on the same total order where the read happened before the write — the order just does not have to match wall-clock. Single-primary async-replicated SQL is sequential but not linearizable; Spanner is linearizable. The gap matters for anything that uses wall-clock causality, such as a check-deposit followed immediately by a balance check.
**Visual:**
```
linearizable:     w1 done @t1 -- real-time -- r2 @t2  => r2 sees w1
sequential:       w1 done @t1 -- real-time -- r2 @t2  => r2 MAY see 0
                 (total order may put r2 before w1, if all clients agree)
```

### Q3. What does causal consistency preserve, and why is it the strongest model available under partitions?
**Answer:** Causal consistency preserves the *happens-before* relation (Lamport, 1978): if operation A causally precedes operation B — because B's issuing client saw the result of A, or B was issued by the same client after A, or there is a chain of such dependencies — then any client that observes B must also observe A. Concurrent operations (those with no causal relationship) can be seen in different orders by different clients. It is the strongest model available under partitions because preserving causality only requires tracking and propagating dependency metadata (vector clocks), not agreeing on a total order. You can serve reads from any replica that has all causally-required writes; you do not need a quorum round or a leader. This is why COPS, Bolt-on Causal, and recent geo-replicated stores like Cure stop at causal rather than going to linearizable. The price is that concurrent writes can conflict, and the application must either resolve them (CRDTs, last-writer-wins) or expose the conflict.
**Visual:**
```
client A:  w1(x=1) -------------------->
client B:           r x=1 ; w2(x=2) --->   (w2 causally after w1)
client C:                          r x=?  -> MUST see >= w1 if sees w2
```

### Q4. Explain read-your-writes, monotonic reads, and monotonic writes. Why are they called "session models"?
**Answer:** Read-your-writes guarantees that a client never reads a value older than what it wrote — if you wrote X=5, subsequent reads return 5 or a later value. Monotonic reads guarantees that a client never sees time go backwards — once you read X=5, you never again read X=3. Monotonic writes guarantees that a client's own writes are seen by all observers in the order it issued them. They are called session models because they apply within a session — a logical context that follows a single user, typically maintained via a session token or sticky routing — and not globally. Amazon DynamoDB and Cassandra implement them by stamping each session with a vector-clock or timestamp watermark and routing reads to replicas whose watermark is at or beyond the session's. They are cheaper than linearizability because they require only session metadata, not global consensus, and they cover most user-facing UX needs: a user always sees their own comment appear, never sees a feed go backwards, and never sees their writes reordered, even while other users may see a slightly stale view.
**Visual:**
```
session(sticky to client U):
  write X=5    -> vector [u=5]
  read X       -> replica must have [u>=5]   (read-your-writes)
  read X again -> never older than previous  (monotonic reads)
  write X=6, then X=7 -> everyone sees 6 before 7 (monotonic writes)
```

### Q5. Why does Cassandra call its consistency "tunable," and what does choosing `QUORUM` actually buy you?
**Answer:** Cassandra lets you set the consistency level on every query — `ANY`, `ONE`, `LOCAL_ONE`, `QUORUM`, `LOCAL_QUORUM`, `ALL` — so each call pays for exactly the durability and freshness it needs. Choosing `QUORUM` means the coordinator waits for acknowledgements from a majority of replicas for that key (with replication factor RF=3, that is 2 of 3). Because read quorums and write quorums always overlap by at least one replica, `QUORUM` reads and `QUORUM` writes together give you strong (linearizable) consistency for that key, modulo the well-known "read-your-writes within a session" caveat handled by `LOCAL_QUORUM` plus read-repair. `LOCAL_QUORUM` restricts the quorum to the local datacenter, which keeps latency low for geo-distributed clusters at the cost of weaker cross-DC consistency. `ALL` is the strongest but most fragile: any replica failure makes the operation fail. The tunability matters because a single Cassandra cluster typically serves many workloads — billing-grade writes at `QUORUM`, analytics at `ONE`, and counter-style updates at `LOCAL_QUORUM` — and paying linearizability cost everywhere would cripple throughput.
**Visual:**
```
RF=3, replicas A,B,C
ONE      -> ack from 1 node        (fast, eventual)
QUORUM   -> ack from 2 of 3        (R+W>RF, strong for this key)
ALL      -> ack from all 3         (strongest, fragile)
```

### Q6. Compare the consistency contracts of Spanner, DynamoDB, Cassandra, and etcd.
**Answer:** Spanner is linearizable globally: every write goes through a Paxos group and waits for TrueTime-bounded uncertainty to pass before commit, giving externally consistent ordering across datacenters. DynamoDB offers two read modes on the same table — `consistentRead=true` (strongly consistent, ~2x read-unit cost, reflects the latest write) and `consistentRead=false` (eventual, may lag by a replica propagation window); writes are always strongly consistent within a region. Cassandra is tunable per query from `ANY` through `ALL`, with `QUORUM`/`QUORUM` yielding strong consistency for a given key. etcd is linearizable for writes via Raft and linearizable for reads either through a quorum round (default `serializable=false`) or through a leader-lease fast path (`serializable=true` returns stale but bounded data). The key contrast is the unit of strong consistency: Spanner is strong across the whole key space, etcd is strong across the whole keyspace but on a small dataset, Cassandra is strong per key at `QUORUM`, and DynamoDB is strong per item only when explicitly requested. Architects pick based on dataset size, latency budget, and per-operation freshness need.
**Visual:**
```
Spanner  : linearizable, global, ~5-7ms commit wait   (CP/EL)
DynamoDB : per-item strong OR eventual, switchable      (tunable)
Cassandra: per-key tunable (ONE..ALL)                   (tunable)
etcd     : linearizable, small keyspace, Raft           (CP/EL)
```

### Q7. What is "stale read" budgeting, and how do you decide the right consistency level for a feature?
**Answer:** Stale-read budgeting is the practice of explicitly deciding, per feature, the maximum staleness a user can tolerate, then choosing the cheapest consistency level that meets the budget. The decision tree starts with the business invariant: is returning a stale value a correctness bug (bank balance, inventory, lock acquisition), a UX bug (comment count slightly behind), or invisible (recommendation feed)? If correctness, pick linearizable — `QUORUM`/`QUORUM` in Cassandra, `consistentRead=true` in DynamoDB, TrueTime-commit in Spanner. If UX, pick session consistency (read-your-writes) plus a bounded staleness like `LOCAL_QUORUM` or a 1-second TTL on a cache. If invisible, pick `ONE` or eventual. The budget must account for both replication lag and clock skew: a 5-second stale budget only works if NTP drift is well below 5 seconds. Netflix, for example, runs the same Cassandra cluster with `LOCAL_QUORUM` for billing-grade playback entitlement and `ONE` for watch history — same cluster, different budgets, because the business cost of staleness differs by four orders of magnitude.
**Visual:**
```
feature               invariant              consistency chosen
billing               never over-charge      linearizable (QUORUM)
comment count         no big visible lag     session + 1s staleness
recommendation feed   invisible              ONE / eventual
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. A social network's "likes counter" runs on Cassandra at `QUORUM`/`QUORUM`. The team finds the cluster cannot keep up with viral post traffic. Propose a redesign that keeps the user experience but doubles throughput.
**Answer:** Likes counters are a textbook eventually-consistent workload — a user seeing 10,003 instead of 10,005 likes for a few seconds is invisible, but charging every like through a quorum round-trip is wasteful. The redesign is: keep per-shard counters in Cassandra at `ONE`/`ONE` (or even `ANY`), bump the write path through a Kafka topic with a 1-second tumbling window so a stream aggregator (Flink/Spark) can batch-increment a per-post counter, and serve reads from a Redis cache populated by the aggregator. Read-your-writes is preserved by having the like API write to both the user's local device state and the Kafka topic, then return the optimistic count, so the user immediately sees their like reflected. Monotonic reads are preserved because the Redis cache is updated only by the aggregator and never regresses. The trade-off is that during a partition, like counts may diverge for a few seconds before converging — acceptable for social signals. The cluster throughput roughly doubles because we removed quorum waits from the hot path, and the design still meets the business invariant (likes are eventually accurate, user sees their own like immediately).
**Visual:**
```
client like -> Kafka(topic=likes, key=post_id) -> aggregator(1s window)
                                                  |
                                                  v
                       Redis(post_id -> count) <--+   <-- reads (ONE)
                            ^
                            |
                  optimistic echo to user (read-your-writes)
```

### Q2. You run a global banking app on DynamoDB. The product team wants to show the user's balance in real time after a transfer. The team proposes `consistentRead=true` on every balance read. Critique the design.
**Answer:** `consistentRead=true` on every balance read is correct but expensive: it consumes twice the read-capacity units of an eventual read and adds the latency of a quorum round on every page load. The cheaper design separates two reads. First, the *post-transfer* read in the same session uses `consistentRead=true` — that is the read-your-writes path, where staleness would be a UX bug ("I just transferred $100, why is the balance unchanged?"). Second, *background* balance reads on app open or dashboard refresh use `consistentRead=false` — eventual consistency is fine because no transfer just happened in this session, and the user is unlikely to notice a 200ms staleness window. To bridge the gap, the client stores the last-known balance plus the last transfer's idempotency key; on app open it does an eventual read, then if a transfer is in-flight it does a single consistent read of just that row. This pattern keeps the consistent-read traffic to ~1% of total reads, cutting DynamoDB cost by roughly half without sacrificing the read-your-writes invariant for the user. The mistake in the original proposal was treating consistency as a property of the table rather than of the read.
**Visual:**
```
after transfer  : consistentRead=true   (1 row, RYW)
dashboard open  : consistentRead=false  (eventual, cheap)
in-flight check : consistentRead=true   (single row, only if needed)
```

### Q3. WhatsApp delivers messages across two datacenters with an active-active design. Two users in different datacenters send messages to the same group at the same instant. How do you keep the conversation coherent?
**Answer:** The two messages are concurrent (no causal relationship) so causal consistency is the natural fit. Each message carries a vector clock reflecting the datacenter's view of the conversation; on delivery, a client replays messages in an order consistent with the vector clocks — if message A's vector is a subset of B's, A is shown before B; otherwise they are concurrent and shown in arrival order with a small "edited above" indicator if needed. Because the workload is conversational, not transactional, the application tolerates two users seeing concurrent messages in slightly different orders for the brief convergence window. The datacenters exchange messages over a low-latency cross-DC link and each applies them to a per-conversation log keyed by conversation id. To preserve read-your-writes, the sending user's own client always echoes their message locally before waiting for cross-DC propagation. The design avoids the cost of global linearizability (which would add 80ms+ to every send) while preserving the only invariants that matter for chat: causality (replies always come after the message they reply to) and session consistency (you see your own message immediately).
**Visual:**
```
DC-A: user1 msg m1, vector [a=5,b=0]   \
DC-B: user2 msg m2, vector [a=0,b=7]    } concurrent, OK to order either way
client: shows m1 then m2 OR m2 then m1 (no causal relation)
reply m3 vector [a=6,b=7] -> MUST come after both m1 and m2
```

### Q4. You are migrating a single-primary PostgreSQL app to a multi-region deployment. The CFO insists that the ledger remains linearizable globally. What architecture do you propose?
**Answer:** A globally linearizable ledger on top of PostgreSQL is the wrong tool — async replication between PG primaries is not linearizable, and synchronous replication across regions adds 80–150ms per write. The right architecture is to put the ledger on a system designed for global linearizability: Google Cloud Spanner, CockroachDB, or YugabyteDB, all of which implement linearizable transactions across regions using Paxos/Raft per shard plus TrueTime-or-equivalent clock uncertainty bounding. The ledger tables live on Spanner with interleaved indexes for hot lookup paths, and writes pay the ~5–10ms commit-wait latency regardless of which region initiates them. For non-ledger features (user profile, recommendations, audit logs), stay on PostgreSQL with async replica reads at `LOCAL` consistency — those workloads do not need linearizability and paying the latency tax for them is wasteful. The migration plan is: extract the ledger service as a separate bounded context, dual-write to PG and Spanner for a validation window, cut reads over to Spanner, then retire the PG ledger. The CFO gets a globally linearizable ledger; the rest of the app keeps its low-latency regional reads.
**Visual:**
```
user profile, recs -> PostgreSQL (regional, async, fast)
ledger, accounts   -> Spanner (global, linearizable, +5-10ms)
                    ^
                    |
              CFO invariant preserved
```

### Q5. etcd is the backing store for Kubernetes. A `kubectl apply` returns success, but a subsequent `kubectl get` returns the old value. Diagnose the consistency mismatch.
**Answer:** This is a stale-read symptom in a system that is supposed to be linearizable, and there are three usual culprits. First, the `kubectl get` may have hit a different apiserver that has not yet observed the etcd commit — Kubernetes apiservers cache etcd state and serve reads from cache unless `resourceVersion=0` is explicitly bypassed or `Cache-Control: no-cache` is set; under load the cache lag is typically <1s but can spike. Second, the client may have a stale list-watch bookmark and is reading from a local cache rather than the apiserver. Third, the etcd read may have been served in `serializable=true` mode (the leader-lease fast path), which can return stale data within the lease window if the leader has changed. The fix is to either (a) read with `?resourceVersion=` set to the value returned by the apply (forcing a read at least as fresh as the write), (b) ensure all apiserver instances are running etcd 3.4+ with linearizable reads enabled by default, and (c) confirm etcd cluster health (`etcdctl endpoint status`) — if a member has fallen behind, evict and re-add it. The diagnosis flow is: check apiserver cache config, check etcd read consistency setting, check etcd member health.
**Visual:**
```
kubectl apply -> apiserver -> etcd commit -> ack
kubectl get   -> apiserver cache (stale)  --> mismatch!
fix: get with resourceVersion >= apply result, OR cache-control: no-cache
```

### Q6. An e-commerce site runs its product catalog on Cassandra at `ONE`/`ONE`. Marketing reports that prices occasionally show as $0 after a price update rolls out. What consistency phenomenon is occurring and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** The $0 is almost certainly a tombstoned or never-written default value being read from a replica that has not yet received the price update — a classic eventual-consistency lag compounded by read-repair timing. With `ONE`/`ONE` and RF=3, a read can land on any of the three replicas; if the price update has propagated to two but not the third, the third returns the older (or default) value. The fix has two layers. First, raise the read consistency to `LOCAL_QUORUM` for price reads — this guarantees reading from at least two replicas, and read-repair will sync the lagging one. Second, the application should never default a missing price to $0 — it should either reject the read or fall back to a cached last-known-good price, because $0 in e-commerce is a business-impacting bug (users will check out for free). The structural fix is to recognize that price is a correctness-critical field and belongs at `LOCAL_QUORUM` or higher, while related fields like reviews and recommendations can stay at `ONE`. The Cassandra tunability model is designed for exactly this per-query trade-off.
**Visual:**
```
price update -> replicas A,B updated, C lags
read at ONE  -> hits C -> returns $0 (or stale)
fix: read at LOCAL_QUORUM -> reads A+B -> max version -> correct price
     + read-repair patches C in the background
```

### Q7. You are designing a collaborative document editor (think Google Docs) for offline-first mobile. Which consistency model do you pick, and how do you handle conflicts when a user reconnects?
**Answer:** A collaborative editor that supports offline editing cannot be linearizable — you cannot refuse writes when the user is on a plane — so the right model is causal-plus-eventual, implemented via CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types). Each document is a CRDT (typically a sequence CRDT like RGA or LSEQ) where every edit is an operation tagged with a logical timestamp and a client id; concurrent edits commute, so when the user reconnects and syncs, both sides converge to the same state without conflict resolution logic. Causal consistency is preserved because operation dependencies (e.g., "insert after character X") are tracked by the CRDT's internal causality metadata, and read-your-writes is trivially satisfied because the local copy reflects every local edit immediately. The trade-off is that CRDTs are more complex than last-write-wins and require careful design for nested structures (rich text, tables), but they are the only model that gives true offline-first behavior. Google Docs itself uses a variant called Operational Transformation for historical reasons, but the modern CRDT-based editors (Yjs, Automerge) demonstrate that this design scales to thousands of concurrent offline users.
**Visual:**
```
offline user edits locally:  op1(insert "Hi", ts=10, client=A)
reconnect: sync ops with server
server has concurrent:        op2(insert "!", ts=11, client=B)
CRDT merge: both ops commute  -> "Hi!" or "!Hi" deterministically
(no conflict resolution needed; converges on every replica)
```
